evidenceLevel: Documentary research except T12: Windows/Chromium extension and local connector have passed unchanged local OpenSSH login, host-key, authorization, terminal, and source-address tests. Broader coverage remains open; see docs/DEVELOPMENT.md.
acceptedImplementation: Ordinary-tab SSH with an extension and local TCP connector is the primary practical path. Optional no-install relay mode requires an explicit relay endpoint and changes source-IP behavior. The stricter helper-free goal remains separate research.
strictGoal: Ordinary unmodified tab; unchanged directly reachable SSH-2 server; no application relay or local bridge; cross-browser interoperability.
scope: 32 candidate mechanisms and variants grouped by architectural boundary; not a proof that every future invention has been enumerated.

options.name: Permissioned TCP API for ordinary tabs
options.reason: Requires browser-vendor changes; no interoperable ordinary-tab TCP API identified.

options.name: WebSocket to an unchanged SSH port
options.reason: HTTP negotiation and WebSocket frames do not match an SSH daemon, regardless of port.

options.name: SSH server with an integrated WSS listener
options.reason: Feed a WebSocket byte stream directly into the server SSH engine; prohibit a second connection to sshd.

options.name: SSH server with integrated WebTransport
options.reason: Requires a compatible target listener and tested browser support; a QUIC socket alone is insufficient.

options.name: SSH server with integrated WebRTC peer
options.reason: Requires target ICE/DTLS/SCTP support; test without TURN and distinguish signaling from session forwarding.

options.name: SSH over paired HTTP streams at target
options.reason: A custom endpoint could join upload requests and a response stream; ordering and latency need evaluation.

options.name: User-supplied WSS byte tunnel
options.reason: SSH stays in the browser while a user-selected service forwards encrypted bytes to the target.

options.name: User-supplied WebTransport tunnel
options.reason: A WebTransport endpoint that dials the SSH target is still a relay.

options.name: WebRTC-to-TCP bridge or TURN route
options.reason: A TCP bridge forwards SSH; TURN forwards the peer traffic. Neither satisfies the strict goal.

options.name: WSS wrapper beside sshd on target
options.reason: Same-machine forwarding to port 22, a pipe, or sshd -i still introduces a bridge.

options.name: Localhost TCP companion
options.reason: An installed local service supplies TCP through HTTP or WebSocket. Installation and a bridge remain.

options.name: Extension plus local TCP connector
options.reason: Accepted primary path, implemented on Windows/Chromium against local OpenSSH: browser WASM SSH uses approved native-messaging byte streams; TCP leaves the user's device under its normal network routing. This does not pass the helper-free goal.

options.name: IWA using Direct Sockets
options.reason: A real raw-TCP reference path; installation, permissions, and platform availability exclude the strict goal.

options.name: Ordinary tab passing bytes through IWA
options.reason: Moving networking to the IWA creates an explicit bridge; do not advertise raw TCP in the tab.

options.name: Custom browser build or privileged flags
options.reason: Can expose sockets in that runtime, but users no longer have ordinary unmodified browsers.

options.name: Electron, Tauri, or embedded webview app
options.reason: Native networking can sit inside an application, but this is an installed client rather than a normal tab.

options.name: Legacy Chrome Apps or retired plugins
options.reason: Historical privileged socket APIs do not supply a supported cross-browser ordinary-tab deployment.

options.name: PWA, service worker, COOP/COEP, shared worker
options.reason: Packaging, isolation, and worker placement do not add an arbitrary TCP primitive.

options.name: WASM SSH or JavaScript SSH alone
options.reason: A protocol engine solves computation, authentication, and channels; it still needs a network byte stream.

options.name: Emulated Linux or user-space TCP stack
options.reason: A virtual NIC still requires an external network backend; in-browser-only networking cannot reach remote hosts.

options.name: Wisp, VPN, or virtual network gateway
options.reason: Encapsulating packets changes the forwarding layer, not the need for a gateway in that architecture.

options.name: WebUSB-controlled network hardware
options.reason: Raw network hardware is a distinct access path, but device permissions, drivers, and browser coverage are unresolved.

options.name: Web Serial modem or PPP device
options.reason: Could expose a physical byte link; requires hardware and a network stack. Serial shell access alone is not SSH.

options.name: Bluetooth or HID networking accessory
options.reason: A custom accessory adds a new dependency; if it forwards to TCP, classify it as a hardware bridge.

options.name: TLS-wrap SSH or move it to port 443
options.reason: Encryption and a different port do not make SSH an HTTP/WebSocket endpoint.

options.name: Fetch CONNECT, HTTP/2 CONNECT, or MASQUE
options.reason: Fetch forbids CONNECT; browser web APIs do not expose a general arbitrary CONNECT tunnel.

options.name: WebSocketStream or ICE-TCP as raw TCP
options.reason: Stream-shaped APIs and TCP under ICE retain their protocol handshakes; they do not expose a generic socket.

options.name: SSH3 / remote terminals over HTTP/3
options.reason: Interesting alternate terminal design; HTTP/3 usage alone does not imply WebTransport compatibility or SSH-2 interoperability.

options.name: Mosh or another terminal protocol
options.reason: Mosh bootstraps through SSH and then uses UDP; it does not remove the browser SSH transport problem.

options.name: ssh URI, remote PTY service, or cloud TCP
options.reason: A remote terminal backend or server-side socket API moves execution outside the browser; a URI opens another client.

options.name: Reverse connection from target
options.reason: Tabs cannot listen for arbitrary inbound TCP; a rendezvous forwarding service is a relay. Direct WebRTC is T05.

options.name: DNS tunnels, parser tricks, or browser exploits
options.reason: Covert channels require cooperating endpoints; browser defects cannot support a portable, maintainable compatibility promise.
